Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Ravi Patel is a 29-year-old house painter who lives with his wife, Priya, in a modest apartment in a midsized Midwestern city. For the past ten months, since the mugging, he has not been the same man she married. The event itself was quick but it carved a lasting groove in his mind. He had been finishing a job in a neighborhood he didn’t know well, a row of older houses with overgrown hedges. It was dusk, and he was walking back to his van, his tool belt slung over his shoulder, when two men stepped out from behind a parked car. One of them held a knife. Ravi remembers the blade glinting under a streetlight, and then the demand for his wallet and phone. He handed them over without a word. That much he knows. But when he tries to deliberately pull back the rest—whether he said anything, whether they said anything else, how he got back to the van—the memory goes fuzzy, like a photograph with the center torn out. What sticks is the guilt. He has come to believe that he should have fought, should have run, should have done something other than stand there frozen. The feeling washes over him every time the memory surfaces, which it does without warning: while he’s mixing paint, while he’s driving home, while he’s lying in bed after a nightmare, the dream residue clinging to him like wet paint. He wakes up with his heart hammering, certain that danger is still there, and it takes Priya shaking his shoulder and saying his name twice before he realizes where he is.

Since the mugging, Ravi’s body has stayed on alert. He feels it in his shoulders, which he keeps hunched, and in his jaw, which he clenches until his teeth ache. He scans constantly. When he arrives at a new job site, he checks every alley, every doorway, every car with its windows down. He has become irritable in ways he never was before—snapping at clients who ask too many questions, getting into a shouting match with a hardware store clerk over a minor price discrepancy. At home, he has pushed Priya away. When she tries to ask how he’s feeling, he cuts her off or leaves the room. He has come to believe that people can’t be trusted, that you can’t rely on anyone. What happened proved it: strangers will hurt you for a few dollars, and there is no safety in numbers or neighborhoods. He feels isolated, set apart from the normal life his friends and family seem to lead. They don’t understand the constant watchfulness, the way a certain street can make his hands shake. He avoids entire sections of the city now, rerouting even if it means adding twenty minutes to his commute. He has lost two regular clients because he refused to work in areas that felt too close to the location where he was mugged. His income has dropped, and he knows Priya is worried, but he cannot bring himself to explain.

What finally brought him to a therapist’s office was a night last week when he woke up from a nightmare—he was back on that street, but this time the knife was at his throat—and he screamed, waking Priya, who found him standing in the corner of the bedroom, his fists raised. For the first time, he saw real fear in her eyes, and it was not fear of the muggers. It was fear of him. The next morning she said, quietly, that he needed help. He agreed, partly because he is exhausted, partly because a small part of him still hopes that someone—a stranger, a professional—can show him how to put the pieces of that night together and stop the guilt from corroding everything. He is afraid that he will never feel safe again, but he is more afraid of losing his wife, his work, and himself piece by piece.
